Local image generation · field notes

Three FLUX models,
one 16 GB GPU

What actually happens when you try to run frontier open-weight image models on a single consumer card. One of them is excellent. One of them is excellent and can’t count. One of them takes four hours per image and had to be deleted.

14 sfastest model
42 smost accurate
~4 hthe 32 B
24×same model, two benchmarks

The rig

One RTX 5060 Ti (16 GB, Blackwell) and 128 GB of system RAM, serving images through an OpenAI-shaped /v1/images/generations endpoint. Every model loads on demand and unloads after 15 idle minutes.

ModelParamsOn diskGPU peak1024² warmVerdict
FLUX.2 klein4 B fp83.8 GB9.4 GB14 sdefault
FLUX.1 dev12 B fp817.2 GB5.7 GB42 saccuracy + 4K
FLUX.2 dev32 B Q4_K_M18.7 GB13.7 GB≈4 hremoved

The 32 B also needs an 11.4 GB text encoder; klein needs a different one again. They are not interchangeable — pairing the wrong encoder fails deep in sampling, never at load.

Getting there

Four moments from the build, with the settings that produced them.

The comparison

Four prompt types chosen to be scoreable rather than admired — exact text, countable objects, stated spatial relations. Same prompts, same seeds, 1024². klein is run twice at different seeds as a variance ruler: its two seeds make near-identical choices on every prompt, so the differences below are signal rather than one lucky sample.

The headline isn’t that the small model is close. It’s that the small model is better at texture and typography — and reproducibly worse at counting.

Portrait

FLUX.1 edges it

prompta close-up portrait of an elderly fisherman with a white beard and weathered skin, wearing a bright yellow raincoat, looking directly at the camera, overcast daylight

All three adhere. FLUX.1 chose the hood up and a warmer key light; klein is correct but flatter.

Rendered text

klein wins

prompta hand-painted wooden shop sign that reads "NORTHWIND BAKERY" in bold serif letters, hanging above a red brick storefront

klein spells it and honours “bold serif” on both seeds. FLUX.1 spells it correctly but returns sans-serif on a painted storefront.

Counting & placement

FLUX.1 wins

promptthree red apples and one green pear on a white marble counter, a blue ceramic mug to the left of the fruit, natural window light from the right

FLUX.1 returns exactly three apples, one pear, mug on the left. klein returns two apples on both seeds — systematic, not luck.

Fine detail

klein wins

promptextreme macro photograph of a dew-covered dragonfly wing at sunrise, iridescent membrane, shallow depth of field

klein reads the brief as true extreme-macro with strong iridescence. FLUX.1 gives a pleasant but conventional macro.

The one that had to go

Same prompt, same night. The 32 B is genuinely better — deeper falloff, more convincing light. It is also 24× the cost, and that was the good measurement.

The first time it was measured, in isolation on a freshly-cleared machine, one 1024² image took 600 seconds. That number was published. Then it was measured again — this time after the two smaller models had already run:

12/24 [2:14:14<1:57:13, 586.10s/it]

That is ~586 seconds per sampling step, not per image: 12 of 24 steps after two and a quarter hours, projecting roughly four hours for one picture. Three prompts in a row timed out and produced nothing.

Both measurements were honest. The difference is the OS page cache. The first run had the model’s own weights still warm in RAM; by the second, the smaller models had filled ~90 GB of cache with theirs, so the 32 B’s ~30 GB was re-read from disk on every step. Same code, same GPU, 24× apart. The bottleneck was never compute — a 32 B transformer plus a 24 B text encoder cannot stay resident on 16 GB, so every step re-uploads the model. No quantization level fixes that: Q3 and Q2 still overflow the card once the encoder is counted.

What the experiment actually bought

Small models fail in specific ways, not general ones

klein beats a model 3× its size on texture and typography, then miscounts “three apples” on both seeds. Capability isn’t a single axis, and a leaderboard number would have hidden this entirely.

A variance ruler costs 30 seconds

Running the cheap model twice at different seeds is what makes a comparison a finding instead of an anecdote. Without it, every claim here is one sample.

Page-cache state can move a benchmark 24×

Benchmark a heavy local model after other models have run, not on a freshly cleared box. The clean-room number is the one you’ll never see in practice.

“It runs” and “it’s usable” are different claims

The 32 B ran. It produced the best image in this whole set. It still had to be deleted, because four hours per image is a science experiment, not a tool.

Reproducing this. FLUX.1 [dev] fp8 at 20 steps, euler / simple, guidance 3.5. FLUX.2 klein 4B fp8 at 24 steps, guidance 4.0. All comparison images 1024 × 1024, seeds as labelled, served through ComfyUI behind an OpenAI-shaped API. Above ~2 MP the request is sampled at the largest native-safe size of the same aspect ratio and upscaled 4×, so “4K” never means “sampled at 4K”.

Every image on this page came off the card described above. No cherry-picking between runs: the comparison grid is the first and only sweep, and the failures are shown as they happened.
